issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: Risky behavior is hard to reconcile with the rest of the threat profile, which is dominated by fear-based hypervigilance and exaggerated startle. In this profile it introduces a more externalizing response pattern that is not supported elsewhere in memory, appraisals, triggers, or strategies.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: Betrayal by a trusted person does not fit well with the stated trauma type of civilian in a war zone unless there is evidence of an interpersonal betrayal trauma, which is otherwise absent from the profile. The rest of the items center on war exposure, victims, grief, loss of control, and danger rather than trusted-person betrayal.

issues.item: Triggers: Victim Memories: Reminders of victims
issues.explanation: Reminders of victims fit war-zone exposure, but paired with perpetrator-focused avoidance and betrayal appraisals they imply a specific interpersonal-harm narrative that is not otherwise coherently represented. The profile oscillates between mass-trauma civilian exposure and a perpetrator-betrayal formulation.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me
issues.explanation: Avoiding cues related to the person who harmed me implies a discrete perpetrator-centered trauma. That is difficult to integrate with the rest of the profile, which more strongly reflects civilian war-zone exposure, victims, grief, and generalized threat rather than a single identifiable assailant.

vignette: Vikram, fifty-three, spent years working as a civilian logistics coordinator in a Middle Eastern conflict zone before a final push through a valley turned a routine supply convoy into a collapse of ground and steel. A sudden explosion tore through the air, a deafening bang that seemed to erase the sky. The impact pinned him beneath a twisted metal panel, knees drawn up, hands braced against the cab floor, utterly unable to direct what happened next. Dust and the sharp, acrid scent of burnt rubber and crushed earth filled his lungs. When the shaking finally stopped, the silence felt heavier than the noise. He walked away, but the valley stayed with him. In the years that followed, his body never stopped bracing. He was perpetually on guard, shoulders tight, jaw clenched, cataloging exits and counting windows. Ordinary noises-a car door slamming, a dropped wrench in his garage, a refrigerator compressor kicking on-made him jump as though shrapnel were flying. When the memories surfaced, his body simply slid back into that pinned position. His knees would lock, his hands would curl into the air, and the old dust would fill his throat. The grief would arrive then, sudden and heavy, overwhelming him until he could not speak. At the same time, the stories would slip away from him, too extreme to be real, too far removed from his quiet life in Cincinnati to belong to him. The tension in his muscles became a second skin, a constant hum of readiness that never faded. He and Priya, his wife, had lived through the accumulating shifts. He took on every painting job he could find, mixing primers, rolling walls, sanding drywall until his fingers ached and the hours blurred. He stopped reading the news, flipping past headlines about foreign conflicts, unwilling to let the broadcasts pull him back. When his mind turned inward, it looped on the same question: why him? He paced his kitchen at night, tracing the same routes, replaying the mechanics of the blast. The world felt like a place that could fall apart without warning, and he knew he was no longer the man who could navigate it. The precision that had once defined him-the steady hand, the even coat, the ability to plan a room's light-felt like a language he had forgotten. Nothing in his life felt meaningful anymore; the work was just noise, the house was just shelter, and the silence between them at dinner grew wider. His work as a painter became a daily confrontation with what he tried to outrun. The thinners and aerosol propellants carried a sharp, chemical bite that mirrored the valley's burnt-dust stench, and on job sites, the crack of a staple gun or the backfire of a delivery truck sent his heart hammering against his ribs. He found himself stepping back from ladders, checking his phone for alerts, and leaving jobs early when a sudden noise echoed through an empty apartment. His wife noticed the way he flinched at ordinary household sounds, the way he started leaving the house before dawn to avoid the evening television broadcast drifting from the living room. The missed deadlines, the unreturned client calls, the distance that stretched between them-these were the quiet changes that settled over their days. What finally brought him to the clinic was not a single collapse, but a Tuesday afternoon when he stood in a half-primed hallway, roller in hand, and felt his knees buckle as a garbage truck backfired outside. He tried to take charge of the cut lines, but the sudden noise shattered his focus and left him paralyzed by a familiar, suffocating lack of control. The smell of wet latex and dust filled his throat, his body locked back into that impossible position, and the grief rose so high it drowned out his own voice. He set the roller down, walked out to his truck, and called the number he had saved weeks ago. He does not know if he will ever feel steady again, and what frightens him most is the certainty that his hands will never hold a brush with the same trust. Yet, beneath that fear, there is a quiet, stubborn hope that somewhere in this room, someone might help him remember how to breathe without bracing.
